steps.body: **100% is the whole itself.** 100% of 60 is 60 — all of it. Less than 100% is part of the whole; MORE than 100% is bigger than the whole: 150% of 20 is 30, because 150/100 × 20 = 30. Percent isn't capped at 100 — it's a rate, and rates can run past the whole.
Fill the entire percent bar to represent the whole.

widget.prompt: The whole bar is worth 60. Fill it to 100% and read the amount represented by the complete bar.
widget.successFeedback: At 100%, the entire 60-unit bar is filled. Therefore 100% of 60 is 60.
widget.lowFeedback: Part of the bar is still empty. Move to 100% to represent the complete whole.
widget.highFeedback: 100% is the full bar and cannot be exceeded in this model.

predict.reveal: Percent means per hundred — and 100 per hundred is everything, exactly once: 100% of 50 is 50, and 100% of 7 is 7, whatever the number. 100% is the identity, the anchor every other percent measures against.

explanationVariants: 150/100 × 20 = 30 — one and a half times the whole.

commonErrors.feedback: 20 is just 100%. The extra 50% adds half again: 20 + 10 = 30.

steps.body: You can also work **backwards**: given a part and its percent, find the whole. If 20% of a number is 8, then the whole is **40** — because 20% is one fifth, and if a fifth is 8, five fifths is 8 × 5 = 40. Check it: 20% of 40 is indeed 8.

explanationVariants: 25% is a quarter, so if a quarter is 9, the whole is 9 × 4 = 36.

widget.prompt: 25% of a number is 9. What is the whole number?

commonErrors.feedback: 9 is the PART (the 25%). The whole is four of those quarters: 9 × 4 = 36.
2.25 rounds oddly — you divided 9 by 4 instead of multiplying. A quarter is 9, so the whole is 9 × 4 = 36.

hints: If a quarter is 9, the whole is 9 × 4.

widget.prompt: Sort each result against its whole.

items.label: 80% of 50
items.feedback: 80% is under 100%, so 80% of 50 (which is 40) is less than 50.

items.label: 120% of 50
items.feedback: 120% is past 100%, so 120% of 50 (which is 60) exceeds 50.

items.label: 200% of 50
items.feedback: 200% is double — 100 — well over the whole of 50.

widget.missFeedback: Compare each percent to 100%: under 100% lands below the whole, exactly 100% equals it, above 100% overshoots. You don't even need the arithmetic.
widget.successFeedback: Sorted — 100% is the dividing line between part and surplus.

explanationVariants: 5% is half of 10%; 10% of 80 is 8, so 5% is 4.

widget.prompt: Estimate with benchmarks: what is 5% of 80?

commonErrors.feedback: 40 is 50% of 80 — a decimal slipped. 5% is half of 10%: half of 8 is 4.
16 is 20% of 80. 5% is much smaller: half of 10% (8) is 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 10% of 80 = 8, and 5% is half of that: 4.

hints: The 15 is the part; 30% is the rate.
If 3/10 of the whole is 15, one tenth is 5.
explanationVariants: 30% of the whole is 15, so 10% is 5 (15 ÷ 3), and the whole (100%) is 5 × 10 = 50.
Break to 10% first: 15 ÷ 3 = 5 per ten percent, times ten = 50.

widget.prompt: 30% of the students in a club is 15 students. How many students are in the whole club?

commonErrors.feedback: 45 adds 30 to 15. Work backwards instead: 30% is 15, so 10% is 5, and 100% is 50.
150 multiplied 15 × 10 — but 15 is 30%, not 10%. First drop to 10%: 15 ÷ 3 = 5, then ×10 = 50.

takeaways: 100% is the whole; under is a part, over exceeds it (150% of 20 = 30).
Work backwards from a part: 20% is 8 means the whole is 40.
steps.teaser: next chapter: ratios as the engine behind every unit conversion.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Rebuild the whole from a part.** If 25% of a number is 7, that 25% is one quarter — so the whole is four quarters: 7 × 4 = 28. The percent tells you how many equal pieces to reassemble.

explanationVariants: 50% is a half, so the whole is 6 × 2 = 12.

widget.prompt: 50% of a number is 6. What is the whole number?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 is the half itself. Two halves make the whole: 6 × 2 = 12.
3 halved the 6 — go the other way. If half is 6, the whole is 6 × 2 = 12.
